articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council approved at its May 3 meeting “traffic-calming” measures at the triangular intersection of Lower Grand Avenue at Grand Avenue, a major arterial within the city. The city will solicit bids for the proposed improvements, not to exceed $75,000. Grand Avenue is a key connector to Oakland on both the southern and northern borders of Piedmont. It also carries the highest traffic volume of any roadway in the city. Seven years ago, in 2014, the location was identified by the city’s Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan as one needing “additional traffic calming,” and was prioritized for improvements due to its unique geometry, explained Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. Plans for improvements were developed by Public Works staff previously, but improvements were delayed due to an East Bay Municipal Utility District [EBMUD] water pipeline project that took more than two years to be completed. City staff’s original intent was to construct a landscaped triangle in the same location as the currently painted triangle in the intersection. It would include subtle directional signage, visible bike lanes, and green infrastructure. However, staff is now considering the “less expensive, but nevertheless effective traffic calming features of painted islands and triangles with reflective bollards Staff photo The Grand Avenue and Lower Grand Avenue intersection was identified by the city’s Pedestrian and Bicycle Master Plan as needing improved signage for motorists. as a way of implementing more traffic calming features sooner and for less cost,” according to a city staff report. In the southbound direction, a new, small triangular-shaped “bulb-out” adjacent to the curb in front of 1608 Lower Grand will be installed, and it will have bollards around its perimeter. Arrows on Grand Avenue will be installed to indicate the direction of traffic for through traffic proceeding north on Grand Avenue. The project will include the installation of “One Way” and “Do Not Enter” pavement markings for the northbound traffic on Lower Grand Avenue adjacent to the new island, and the installation of new red curbing on the nose of the existing island. articles.text: 95% of Piedmont residents are vaccinated Young Californians ages 12 to 15 could start receiving doses of COVID-19 vaccine as early as tomorrow, Thursday, May 13. On Monday, May 10, the Food and Drug Administration expanded the emergency use authorization offered to vaccine manufacturer Pfizer so that its vaccine can be used in children ages 12 to 15. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is scheduled to discuss this new authorization today, May 12. Additionally, the Western States Scientific Advisory Group is expected to vote today on the updated guidelines for California. Vaccines could start going into the arms of this new age group a day after approval is issued. The new authorization means all high schoolers and most middle schoolers will be eligible for vaccination. Vaccinations continue apace in Alameda County. Almost 1.6 million vaccine doses have been administered countywide, and over 52 percent of adults in Alameda County are now fully vaccinated. Piedmont is the most vaccinated municipality in the county by a large margin. The City is approaching some experts’ definitions of so-called “herd immunity,” a point when enough people are immune to a disease, either through vaccination or infection, that its spread is reduced. Initial estimates suggested that COVID-19 herd immunity would be reached when 60 to 70 percent of a population is immune, although more recent estimates suggest that immunity might need to be as high as 90 percent. Alameda County has said that its goal is to vaccinate at least 70 to 80 percent of the county. In Piedmont, 95 percent of residents ages 16 and older, some 8,112 people, have received at least one dose of vaccine, as of Monday. Over 72 percent of the City’s adults, about 6,175 people, have been fully vaccinated. Hesitancy surrounding the COVID-19 vaccine in Alameda County is about 9 percent – below national averages, according to polls released in April by the Department of Health and Human Services. Only 3.4 percent of those polled in the county said they were strongly hesitant. As a small city, vaccination will have to increase across Alameda County before herd immunity is really reached in the region. In Oakland, 70 percent of the adult population is partially vaccinated and 50 percent are fully vaccinated. Three vaccines are available in the United States, but only the Pfizer vaccine has been approved by the FDA for those age 12 and older. Pfizer and Moderna vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. A vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson, which is back in use after being paused due to rare blood clotting concerns, requires only one dose. The Moderna and Johnson & Johnson vaccines are approved for adults ages 18 and older. Both Pfizer and Moderna are currently conducting vaccine trials in children as young as 6 months old. Dr. Anthony Fauci, the Chief Medical Advisor to the White House, said this week that he expected all children will be eligible for vaccination by the end of the year. On April 12, Alameda County opened COVID-19 vaccination appointments to all residents. As of press time, same-day appointments were available at several locations in Oakland and elsewhere in the county. Alameda County links to available vaccine appointments at covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines The state has administered about 32.9 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of almost 264,000 people per day. Almost 14.5 million Californians, about 46 percent of the adult population, have been fully vaccinated. The rate of positive cases of COVID-19 in California dropped to a record low of 1 percent as of Monday, May 10. The rolling seven-day positivity rate in Alameda County, now 1.2 percent, was only slightly higher. Since March 10, the county’s positivity rate has been lower than at any other point of the 14-month pandemic. Alameda County has yet to meet state benchmarks to move into a less-restrictive tier for reopening its economy, but metrics are moving in the right direction. Since March 30, Alameda County has been in the orange tier, or moderate tier, the second-least restrictive tier in California’s color-coded four-tier system. Last Tuesday, May 4, San Francisco County was moved into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier. Yesterday, Tuesday, May 11, San Mateo County became the second Bay Area county to be moved into the yellow tier. Most indoor activities can resume, with modification, in the yellow tier. To move into the yellow tier, the positivity rate in Alameda County needs to stay below 2 percent. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 2.2 percent – it is currently 1.6 percent in Alameda County. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1 – right now there are 2.9 cases per 100,000, a drop from last week but still above the benchmark. The entire color tier system is planned to be closed in about a month. Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans several weeks ago to lift most COVID-19 restrictions statewide on June 15. It is expected that the reopening plan will continue if hospitalizations remain low and vaccination supply is not majorly disrupted. California ranks 49th in the nation in terms of where the coronavirus is spreading the fastest, according to data from Johns Hopkins University. On Monday, May 10, the Food and Drug Administration expanded the emergency use authorization offered to vaccine manufacturer Pfizer so that its vaccine can be used in children ages 12 to 15. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is scheduled to discuss this new authorization today, May 12. Additionally, the Western States Scientific Advisory Group is expected to vote today on the updated guidelines for California. Vaccines could start going into the arms of this new age group a day after approval is issued. The new authorization means all high schoolers and most middle schoolers will be eligible for vaccination. Vaccinations continue apace in Alameda County. Almost 1.6 million vaccine doses have been administered countywide, and over 52 percent of adults in Alameda County are now fully vaccinated. Piedmont is the most vaccinated municipality in the county by a large margin. The City is approaching some experts’ definitions of so-called “herd immunity,” a point when enough people are immune to a disease, either through vaccination or infection, that its spread is reduced. Initial estimates suggested that COVID-19 herd immunity would be reached when 60 to 70 percent of a population is immune, although more recent estimates suggest that immunity might need to be as high as 90 percent. Alameda County has said that its goal is to vaccinate at least 70 to 80 percent of the county. In Piedmont, 95 percent of residents ages 16 and older, some 8,112 people, have received at least one dose of vaccine, as of Monday. Over 72 percent of the City’s adults, about 6,175 people, have been fully vaccinated. Hesitancy surrounding the COVID-19 vaccine in Alameda County is about 9 percent – below national averages, according to polls released in April by the Department of Health and Human Services. Only 3.4 percent of those polled in the county said they were strongly hesitant. As a small city, vaccination will have to increase across Alameda County before herd immunity is really reached in the region. In Oakland, 70 percent of the adult population is partially vaccinated and 50 percent are fully vaccinated. Three vaccines are available in the United States, but only the Pfizer vaccine has been approved by the FDA for those age 12 and older. Pfizer and Moderna vaccines require two doses administered several weeks apart. A vaccine produced by Johnson & Johnson, which is back in use after being paused due to rare blood clotting concerns, requires only one dose. The Moderna and Johnson & Johnson vaccines are approved for adults ages 18 and older. Both Pfizer and Moderna are currently conducting vaccine trials in children as young as 6 months old. Dr. Anthony Fauci, the Chief Medical Advisor to the White House, said this week that he expected all children will be eligible for vaccination by the end of the year. On April 12, Alameda County opened COVID-19 vaccination appointments to all residents. As of press time, same-day appointments were available at several locations in Oakland and elsewhere in the county. Alameda County links to available vaccine appointments at covid-19.acgov.org/vaccines The state has administered about 32.9 million vaccine doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of almost 264,000 people per day. Almost 14.5 million Californians, about 46 percent of the adult population, have been fully vaccinated. COVID-19 positivity rates in California drop to 1 percent San Mateo County joins San Francisco in yellow tier; Alameda County still in orange tier activities and crowded outdoor spaces will likely remain in place until further notice. No new cases of COVID-19 were reported in Piedmont in the past week, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. The total number of Piedmont cases since the pandemic began is 181. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 87,733 – an increase of 407 new cases weekover-week. There have been 27,300 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,612 cases in Hayward. Tragically, 13 more people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 1,551. On May 3, California officially adopted masking guidance that follows new recommendations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention that said people fully vaccinated against the COVID-19 virus do not need to wear masks outdoors anymore unless they are in a crowd of strangers. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since either their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,656,967 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 61,246 deaths due to the disease statewide. By Barry Eitel The rate of positive cases of COVID-19 in California dropped to a record low of 1 percent as of Monday, May 10. The rolling seven-day positivity rate in Alameda County, now 1.2 percent, was only slightly higher. Since March 10, the county’s positivity rate has been lower than at any other point of the 14-month pandemic. Alameda County has yet to meet state benchmarks to move into a less-restrictive tier for reopening its economy, but metrics are moving in the right direction. Since March 30, Alameda County has been in the orange tier, or moderate tier, the second-least restrictive tier in California’s color-coded four-tier system. Last Tuesday, May 4, San Francisco County was moved into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier. Yesterday, Tuesday, May 11, San Mateo County became the second Bay Area county to be moved into the yellow tier. Most indoor activities can resume, with modification, in the yellow tier. To move into the yellow tier, the positivity rate in Alameda County needs to stay below 2 percent. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 2.2 percent – it is currently 1.6 percent in Alameda County. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1 – right now there are 2.9 cases per 100,000, a drop from last week but still above the benchmark. The entire color tier system is planned to be closed in about a month. Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans several weeks ago to lift most COVID-19 restrictions statewide on June 15. It is expected that the reopening plan will continue if hospitalizations remain low and vaccination supply is not majorly disrupted. California ranks 49th in the nation in terms of where the coronavirus is spreading the fastest, according to data from Johns Hopkins University. articles.text: The Piedmont community is invited to attend two upcoming Housing Advisory Committee meetings on Wednesday, May 19, and June 15. The newly formed Housing Advisory Committee was created by City Council earlier this year to provide feedback on documents prepared throughout the city’s housing programs project, and the housing element update process. The committee meets as needed and terminates upon the receipt by City Council of a draft Housing Element Update document. The committee consists of Rani Batra, June Catalano, Jane Lin, Justin Osler, and Claire Parisa. Planning Director Kevin Jackson serves as staff liaison. The meeting on May 19 will feature results of the city’s fair housing survey and pinnable map. Both were made accessible to residents on March 12, and the survey was available through April 15. The survey is one of several opportunities throughout the 18-month, city-led effort to ensure that new housing in Piedmont is feasible to develop, high in quality, and affordable. In the next Regional Housing Needs Cycle (RHNA), Piedmont is tasked with creating 587 housing units, compared to 60 units in the current RHNA cycle, representing a 979 percent increase. On March 2, city council issued a Request for Proposal [RFP] seeking a consulting firm to assist it in meeting the next RHNA planning period, which falls between 2023 and 2031. On May 3, City Council approved a proposal from Lisa Wise Consulting (LWC) to update the Housing Element of the city’s general plan. The consultant is expected to present the analysis of Piedmonters’ design preferences, understanding of housing laws, and other ideas drawn from the survey. The consulting firm will also provide recommendations for guiding principles for new tools to accelerate housing production. In addition, the first meeting will include a briefing on the Housing Element 2015 - 2022 annual progress report and a discussion of next steps and plans for a future community workshop. It will also include the election of a chair and vice chair of the committee. Agendas and instructions for participating in both Zoom meetings, which begin at 5 p.m., are posted on the city’s website at: https://piedmont.ca.gov/government/commissions___committees/housing_advisory_committee. The two meetings will be televised live on KCOM-TV, the City’s government TV station (Channel 27), and will be available through streaming video on the City’s web site: https://piedmont.ca.gov/services___departments/kcom-tv/live_content_ and_video_archive. For more information and project updates, visit the City’s website at: https://piedmont. ca.gov/, or contact Senior Planner Pierce Macdonald-Powell (pmacdonald@piedmont.ca.gov).

articles.text: Transportation is one of the two largest causes of greenhouse gas emissions in the City of Piedmont. As you may guess, this stems largely from gas powered cars. Driving is not unique to Piedmont. Transit is the largest emissions category for California and the U.S. Bay Area drivers collectively clock over 170 million miles every day. For environmental planners, emissions from driving obviously is a priority. Vehicle miles travelled, one metric used to measure usage, has been steadily climbing for years nationwide. Although 2020 has fewer VMT’s due to COVID, the larger issue still remains – people rely on driving to get around. They will continue to drive more unless something changes. How can governments convince residents to drive less? At the local government level, there are a few tools up our sleeves. One method is to change the built environment. Visit any street with lots of car traffic and you’ll notice something: the car lanes are a lot bigger than the sidewalks and bike lanes. Drivers respond to their environment. If a trip is easiest to take by driving, cars are going to be the main way people get to and from their destination. By using planning, we can make other methods of transportation more appealing, and hopefully increase those methods. Every person who takes the bus or walks means one fewer less car on the road. You can see how planning impacts commuting habits with highway construction. One common proposed way to deal with traffic has been to widen roadways. Study after study has shown that wider roadways eases traffic – but only temporarily. Five to ten years after the widening, traffic is back to its normal levels, and the road is wider, meaning more cars, and more pollutants (in economics, this phenomenon is “induced demand”). If you build it, they will come! The inverse of this is to expand oppor t u nities for non-drivers. Piedmont Public Works is always working on more sustainable solutions. Improving bike lanes and sidewalks are great examples of ways to offer alternatives that will entice people to change their habits. Other examples include “bulbouts,” which encourage cars to slow down around corners, speed bumps, improved signage, and enhanced crosswalk visibility. The list goes on. Many of these techniques have real effects on driving and walking habits. Another way to get people to change their driving habit is to make alternatives more appealing, either through cost or time savings, or having people associate alternatives with their values. In electric vehicle ads, you will often see monetary savings advertised, but there is usually environmental messaging as well. Manufacturers know that some buyers will be interested in having a smaller carbon footprint in addition to saving money. You can also change the building code to make electric vehicle charging easier for homeowners. Although encouraging people to use public transit, biking, and walking is a priority, driving will not go away overnight. The City of Piedmont tries to encourage drivers to switch to electric vehicles because they can use our carbon free electricity to charge, meaning far fewer emissions than a normal car. Ultimately, it is up to individuals how they choose to travel, but the built environment can help people make up their minds. Piedmont is hilly, but there is a lot of bike infrastructure in our little city. I encourage you to give it a try. If you have questions about electric vehicles, charging, or anything else related to sustainability, please reach out to Nate at nredinbo@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: The Bay Area “Bike to Wherever Day,” which replaces the popular “Bike to Work Day” due to the COVID-19 pandemic, will take place on Friday, May 21. Traditionally, Bike to Work Day is a celebration of cycling as a sustainable and healthy way to get to work, and serves as an opportunity for those who don’t usually bike commute to try it out. Many Piedmont residents and city staff participate in the event. Due to the prolonged pandemic, this year the event returns as Bike to Wherever Day. Make a pledge to ride and join other Bay Area residents by visiting https://bikeeastbay.org/events/bike-wherever-day-2021 before the day of the event. By signing up, you’ll receive a map of energizer stations, a digital goody bag, and suggested bicycle routes in Alameda County. You’ll receive a limited-edition tote bag at a contact-free energizer station this year. The East Bay Bike coalition also includes tips for new riders, opportunities to take free classes, and more digital resources.

articles.text: Sunday, May 2, was a splendid day for some service and adventure for Troop 6 Scouts. Working as the guest crew on the sailing ship SeaValor under the command of Eric Jones, the Scouts spent a beautiful day on the Bay learning and practicing seamanship skills, like piloting, setting and maintaining sails, as well as navigating the busy Bay. The Scouts also worked on their search and rescue skills, including visual search patterns as well as victim recovery. The sailing ship did numerous man-overboard drills with their certified rescue bear – a large stuffed bear fitted with a life jacket that mimics the weight and size of an overboard child. Upon arrival at Angel Island, patrols of scouts were dispatched A large group of Scouts from Troop 6 come onto land at a secluded spot on Angel Island to do some service Two Boy scouts from Piedmont’s Troop 6 test their navigational skills on the bowsprit of the SeaValor. by a Zodiac launch to a series of boat-in only beaches to collect trash and debris. During this activity, a dead gray whale was spotted floating in the shipping channel. SeaValor leaped into action, capturing the carcass and towing it to shore at a secluded beach for later review by the Marine Mammal Center. After this excitement, the SeaValor traveled to another boat-in beach for a scout-cooked lunch, waterplay, and exploration. While on the beach, more whales were spotted, but these whales were alive and active, feasting in the strong currents of the Racoon Straits between Tiburon and Angel Island. All in all, this was another memorable Troop 6 adventure.
articles.title: Troop 6 Scouts sail, work in day on the Bay

articles.text: The Piedmont Makers hosted the Annual Maker Faire on Saturday, May 8. Even with the socially-distanced event spread across the city, Piedmont’s vibrant maker community eagerly embraced a day filled with inventive DIY spirit, complete with car crashes, course changes, robotic exhibitions, and more. A Nerdy Derby racetrack was set up at Beach, Havens, and Wildwood schools. At each elementary school stop kids gravitated to tables of spare parts and decor and designed and refined their cars for speed and aesthetics. Different stops developed different themes on their own. Makers at Wildwood, as example, collected different (and ever larger) rocks to add weight and speed. A student at Beach built a jump that became a permanent track fixture. Cars did flips and occasionally landed on the other track, but almost all managed to keep going. Nerdy Derby cars were as varied as the participants. Cars featured battery-powered LED headlights, a laser-engraved car name, a banana bread body, minifigure drivers, a root beer bottle, custom-cut aerodynamic car bodies, wheels lubricated with graphite and silicone, and a balloon car. Kids and parents alike enjoyed the opportunity to exercise their creative spirit in an open, inventive, and supportive environment. At the robotics demo, people explored some of the cutting-edge maker technology that will soon populate the Piedmont Engineering Lab in the high school’s new STEAM building. The FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) team members demoed their robots’ amazing dexterity and shooting capabilities. For those who were more comfortable maintaining distance, the Piedmont Makers organized five Maker Faire At-Home projects. Kids (and parents) built homemade Water Blasters using PVC pipes, designed Paper Circuit Cards just in time for Mother’s Day, made Glow-in-the-Dark Lava Lamps, balanced found objects into surprisingly stable sculptures, and made spinning Lego® tops. Project instructions will remain on the Makers website (piedmontmakers.org) for Makers to enjoy. The Piedmont Makers were very excited to share the Maker spark with the community through this year’s distributed event. articles.text: Piedmont Boy Scouts JD Harrison, Alex Hilton, and Nicky Allen-Goix will attain the rank of Eagle at a National Court of Honor cereemony on May 15. Three Piedmont Boy Scouts from Troop 1 – JD Harrison, Alex Hilton, and Nicky AllenGoix – will be presented with the rank of Eagle Scout on May 15 at 3:30 p.m. in a National Court of Honor ceremony at the amphitheater behind the Piedmont Community Center. Harrison and Hilton began their scouting journey in elementary school, moving from Cub Scouts to Webelos and finally, onto Boy Scouts. Allen-Goix joined them in Troop 1 as a 7th grader and quickly became an integral part of the Troop. As they grew in age, so did their responsibilities, leadership, and service roles and experiences. They advanced through the ranks of Tenderfoot, Second Class, First Class, Star, Life, and finally, to Eagle. In addition to the 21 merit badges required to achieve the rank of Eagle, a scout must accomplish a service project which involves hours of planning, developing and leading others to help with its implementation. Often Eagle projects are chosen because of personal importance to the scout. All three dedicated their projects to students with fewer resources and opportunities. Allen-Goix created 50 backpacks filled with school supplies matching the list that first grade teachers at Cox Academy said each child needed for pandemic distant learning. The school serves a low-income population in Oakland. Harrison built three planter boxes to be used as an educational garden at the Booth Memorial Center Childcare in Oakland, which provides childcare for houseless families. Hilton built three planter boxes and a connecting bench for James Baldwin Academy, a middle school in Alameda for learning disabled children. All three Scouts are grateful for all the help they received from Troop 1 adult leaders, from their Eagle advisors, their fellow scouts and friends who helped them achieve this milestone in their scouting careers.
articles.title: Troop 1 celebrates 3 more Eagle Scouts

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council approved a contract in the amount of $118,504 with AVI SPL to enhance the city’s police department audio and visual capabilities. The contract will allow audio and visual enhancement for daily briefings, training, presentations, web conferencing and public information. Key areas that will be enhanced in the department include the briefing room, sergeants’ office, and police department public lobby. The police will outfit each of the spaces with digital video displays within an integrated system. It is expected to provide better communication and information to the public, as well as support the department’s critical work. The briefing room will be equipped with a multi-window display of content feeds, and the Sergeants’ office will be outfitted with a wall-mounted flat-panel display for web conferencing. AVI SPL was the lowest of two bidders for the contract. Community Oriented Policing Services (COPS) funds, from the 2020-2021 state budget, also will help fund the project. The girls’ basketball team remained undefeated at 7-0 after a busy week with five more victories, improving its record to 7-0 after recording five wins in the last seven days. Three were against non-league teams and two were WACC Foothill Division games. Results include a 49-44 win at Binks Rawlings Gym against Marin Catholic on Monday, May 10; a one-sided 68-28 win against San Marin on May 8 also at home; a 62-66 victory over San Leandro on the road on May 7; another rollover win, 65-25 against Alameda at home on May 5; and a surprisingly easy 62-36 over California on May 4. The most impressive win came against Marin Catholic, a perennial post-season playoff team in Piedmont’s Div. 4 North Coast Section bracket. They were the No. 3 seed in last year’s NCS playoffs. “We knew that Marin Catholic would be really tough, but our senior, Nakilah [Kai Johnson], really led us. This game was probably more fun than the others. Marin Catholic is a good Div. 4 team, and we love the competition,” said coach Bryan Gardere Each of Piedmont’s other opponents last week rank above PHS in the NCS divisions, California and San Leandro are Division 1, Alameda is Div. 2, and San Marin is Div. 3. All have larger enrollments than Piedmont, but the Highlanders’ level of talent made the difference. “We really picked it up at halftime and kept our composure. We attacked the basket and started getting points and free throws. Piedmont’s defense then held Marin Catholic without a score for four minutes and limited them to 7 points in the final quarter. A Johnson free throw gave Piedmont a 45-44 lead, and freshman Natalie Martinez scored the final four points on a pair of free throws and layup on a pass from Brie Sotelo. articles.text: This is the last weekend to visit the 7th annual Juried Art Show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. It will be open on Saturday and Sunday May 15-16 from 12 p.m. to 2 p.m. A total of 35 pieces of art were selected by two guest jurors from a record-high 500 submissions. The artwork appearing in the exhibition, the first public event PCA has held this year, was selected by Rene de Guzman, Senior Curator of Art at Oakland Museum of California, and Danielle Fox, Principal of Slate Gallery in Oakland. Artists from nine counties in the greater Bay Area were invited to enter the competition, resulting in an eclectic range of artwork, including oil on canvas, pigment prints, and photography, The Juried Art show debuted in November 2013, PCA Board Member Valerie Corvin explained. The annual event is made possible through the John P. Thornborrow Memorial Fund, which was created to support local artists and is distributed as a cash prize to three selected artists. Thornborrow was a Bay Area artist who created hundreds of artwork across a variety of mediums. In 2008, Thornborrow’s work was selected for the Pro Arts Juried Annual, which was juried by Laura Hoptman, Senior Curator of the New Museum in New York. He continued to produce artwork until his death in 2011; his print, “Fake Flowers,” hangs as part of the Juried Art Show exhibit. “Every year, the Juried Art Staff photo The 7th annual Juried Art Show ends this Sunday at the Center for the Arts. show aims to give emerging artists from the Bay Area an opportunity to gain exposure with top curators and gallerists and the general public,” explained Corvin. “Thanks to the John P. Thornborrow Memorial Endowment Fund, total cash awards of $4,000 [are] allocated to juror-designated award winners. First place winner Pep Ventosa was awarded $2,500 for “Watching the Night Sky.” Second place for $1,000 went to Tamara Avery for “#114 Justice?,” and See C Oh took third place and $500 for “Tranquility.” Three honorable mentions were also awarded: Brian Molyneaux’s photo on a metal sheet, “Moon, Neferttiti, Barry”; Nelson Loskamp’s “Cay on the Beach;” and Daniel San Souci’s “Flight of the Monarchs.” Honorable mentions received ribbons. Corvin said that the selections this year produced the “best Juried Art Show yet” in the event’s seven-year existence at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. “The art is a high level, and it feels like you are in a downtown art gallery, it’s very exciting,” she added. Visitors should sign up in advance for a time slot at https:// bit.ly/3mwWuwT. Gallery viewers will be asked to sanitize hands upon entry, wear face masks, and observe social distancing. For more information, see www.piedmontcenterforthearts. org. Napoleon Bonaparte Ludwig van Beethoven Niccolo Paganini had the talent of genius and the morals of an ape. Another apocryphal story tells us that Napoleon tried to play the cello. The most famous cellist of the time had just completed a command performance. After the cellist finished his performance, Napoleon asked to try to play the same cello himself. The story goes that his spurs put some gauges in the cello. Wouldn’t you know it… That cello became the most expensive Stradivarius in the world. The great musical liberator Beethoven was so inspired by Napoleon that he dedicated his colossal Third Symphony to the Frenchman. When Napoleon crowned himself Emperor, Beethoven obliterated the name of Napoleon from the title page. His rage was so furious that he made a hole in the paper. Up until then, Beethoven had faith that Napoleon would be the great leader for all of mankind. Paganini‘s connection with Napoleon is somewhat oblique. He was hired to be the violin soloist to Napoleon’s sister. During his employ, he dedicated at least two of his most important compositions to the emperor. One was the “Napoleon Sonata” which caused a sensation because it was played entirely on one string. No violinist had ever done this before. The other famous composition also caused a sensation. It is known today as Duetto Amoroso. Even though it was written as a birthday present for Napoleon, Paganini really intended it as a love letter to his employer. As you can guess, Paganini was more interested in love than in politics. All of these three great men knew that music has the greatest effect on the emotions. Napoleon spoke for all when he said: “music is the soul of love, the sweetness of life, the consolation for sorrow, and the companion of innocence.“ That’s about all that needs to be said. And now for present times After such a long time, concert life is showing signs of rejuvenation. My wife and I attended a concert in Saint Mary’s Cathedral on Sunday as performed by the “Quantum Quintet.” Traffic over the bridge to San Francisco was miserable, but the concert was a delight. We missed the first number on the program but we did enjoy Dvorak’s superb Piano Quintet. The musicians were pianist Jeanette Wilkin Tieze, violinists Wendy Loder and Odin Mitaine, violist Meg Eldridge, and cellist Joel Cohen. Throughout the performance, the musicians were ever-alert to the musical exigencies of the spirit of the music. The expressive second movement was particularly heartfelt. The fast scherzo movement was taken at a conservative tempo, proving that it is not necessary to play fast and loud to be effective. This type of playing should serve as a good example to other performers who seem to think that the faster and louder they play the greater will be the ovation. Napoleon’s advice should be the guideline: Music is the soul of love.

articles.text: Soprano Vanessa Becerra will be featured in Opera San Jose’s recital program on May 14, Opera San Jose, in partnership with Los Angeles Opera, has created a recital program featuring Latina composers. The program was prepared with the assistance of Indiana University’s Latin American Music Center and will stream on Facebook and YouTube on May 14, after which it will be available on-demand. The program is curated by Los Angeles Opera Artist in Residence Russell Thomas, and features Opera San Jose resident company members. It will include songs by Maria Luisa Escobar, Consuelo Velazquez, Modesta Bor, and Angela Peralta. Four contemporary composers, Gabriela Lena Frank, Tania Leon, Mariela Rodriguez, and Irma Urteaga, will be represented. The featured performers in the Latina Composers recital are soprano Vanessa Becerra, tenor Enrique Santelli, and baritone Efrain Solis. Becerra and Santelli are both alumni of Los Angeles Opera’s Domingo-Colburn-Stein Young Artist Program. “The songs celebrate an incredibly rich and diverse range of musical works created by Latinas over the past two centuries throughout the Americas,” said Thomas. “Their music will transport audiences to Mexico, Venezuela, Argentina, Cuba, and Peru, all while honoring the women who wrote each piece. It was fantastic to partner with the incredible team at Opera San Jose on this gorgeous new project.” You can sign up for the livestream by visiting: https://www. operasj.org/latina-composers-recital/.
articles.title: Opera San Jose recital program to feature Latina composers May 14

articles.text: This is the last weekend to watch San Francisco Opera’s production of The Barber of Seville, the company’s first live production since the health pandemic closed venues last year. The new, 90-minute adaptation of Rossini’s romantic comedy is sung in English. This performance will feature Lucas Meachem as Figaro, Daniela Mack as Rosina, Alek Shrader as Almaviva and Philip Skinner as Doctor Bartolo, with music performed by the San Francisco Opera Orchestra. “The Barber” is an opera buffa in two acts, and is widely regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of comedy within music. The play follows the story of a cunning barber who helps a young ward escape from the custody of her guardian, and into the arms of a noble suitor. The opera is directed by Matthew Ozawa. The final performances are Friday and Saturday, May 14 and 15. Both performances will be drive-in productions held at Marin Center in San Rafael. articles.text: Cast members rehearse for Youth Musical Theater Company’s production of 13 the Musical opening May 22 in Berkeley. Youth Musical Theater Company (YMTC) presents 13 the Musical for six performances from May 22–30. It will be the third Covid-compliant musical the company has produced during the pandemic. After their March 2020 production of The Music Man was shut down mid-run, YMTC asked their donors to help raise funds to build an outdoor stage at its Aquatic Park rehearsal space in order to continue offering in-person programming. In October 2020, they produced The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee with a small audience of family members on the stage. This February, they produced a concert version of Sondheim’s Merrily We Roll Along with a slightly larger audience sitting on newly built outdoor bleachers. Now, using updated state and county Covid requirements and with a teenage cast that is half-vaccinated and a creative team and crew that is fully vaccinated, they are highlighting 13 young artists in this delightful and funny musical. Jason Robert Brown’s jazzy pop-rock score tells the classic story of coming-of-age against all odds. Professional directors, designers and technicians work alongside the student both onstage and off as part of the Theater Arts Apprentice Program (TAAP). The six piece band features professional Bay Area musicians, led by music director Jon Gallo, and includes Piedmont High freshman Miranda Long on guitar. “It is always especially exciting when we can produce a musical that places teenagers at the center of its story. It is surprising how few musicals do this, given the popularity of musical theater among young people,” said YMTC Artistic Director Jennifer Boesing. Due to the limited audience size and social distancing requirements, all shows are now sold out. YMTC will return in July with Light in the Piazza. For more information, visit: ymtcbayarea.org.
articles.title: YMTC brings live theater back to Berkeley

articles.text: Aurora Theatre Company is presenting an audio play adaption of Toni Morrison’s novel, The Bluest Eye, available to stream now through May 21. Jeff Orlowski’s award-winning documentary, The Social Dilemma, will be the subject of a discussion hosted by Piedmont’s long-r unning Appreciating Diversity Film Series. A discussion with UC Berkeley Law Professor Rebecca Wexler will take place on Thursday, May 13 at 5:00 p.m. Viewers can watch the film at their convenience anytime on Netflix or can register for the May 13 discussion and receive a link to get free access to the film on Netflix. A free link will be sent to anyone who requests one from christy@diversityfilmseries.org. That link will work anytime over the next several months. Sign up for the discussion on diversityfilmseries.org and click on “Register for The Social Dilemma.” The film documents the hidden practices that underlie the business of social media. Viewers will learn that the algorithms designed to capture your attention are also profoundly affecting your brains and beliefs in ways that directly threaten democracy. An internal Facebook report by sociologist Monica Lee states, “64% of the people who joined extremist groups on Facebook did so because the algorithms steered them there.” Other documentaries have raised concerns about the impact of social media on privacy and even democracy. This film’s advantage is that the speakers in The Social Dilemma include top executives from Twitter, Instagram, Pinterest, Facebook, and others. The experts assure us their intentions were good– even the one whose job title at Facebook was head of “monetization”. Yet all are deeply concerned about what they’ve created, and one confesses that he worked all day on making his site irresistibly seductive and then found himself unable to resist the very algorithmic tricks he helped to create when he went home at night. The most important lesson from the film is that people should question everything they read online, especially if it is presented in a way that reflects a detailed understanding of personal inclinations and preferences. Viewers should learn to resist the “attention extraction model” that makes social media seem friendly and reinforcing. As the New York Times has advised, “Unplug and run”. After viewing The Social Dilemma, join the Diversity Film Series audience for Q & A discussion with Rebecca Wexler, Assistant Professor of Law at UC Berkeley Law, and Co-Director of the Berkeley Center for Law & Technology. Wexler teaches, researches, and writes on issues concerning data, technology, and criminal justice. The Appreciating Diversity Film Series is co-sponsored by the City of Piedmont, Piedmont League of Women Voters and Piedmont School District.

articles.text: Free Solo follows Alex Honnold as he climbs El Capitan in Yosemite National Park. Free Solo is a National Geographic documentary film, directed by award-winning filmmaker Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and shot by world-renowned photographer and mountaineer Jimmy Chin. It is a stunning and unflinching portrait of professional mountain climber Alex Honnold and focuses primarily on his obsessive preparation to fulfill a lifelong dream. His goal is to climb the face of the world famous 3,200-foot El Capitan in Yosemite National Park without safety gear. What “free” means is that such a climb surpasses all definitions of extreme sports, existing in a realm that defies all explication and enters into the mystical, a silent meditation on life – or death. To climb El Capitan solo and survive is one of the greatest athletic feats of any kind. There is nothing else in sports that compares. The actual filming of such an attempt is also breathtaking in its beauty and sustained sense of risk (and vertigo). It’s beautiful. There is also a sense of controlled and disciplined panic on the part not only of Honnold but of Chin and the film crew. It is quietly gripping, conveyed with each harrowing pitch on the ascent up the granite face. To climb solo at such heights is to exist in the zone of the unblemished, beyond anything that can be imagined. To attempt such a climb is to celebrate life intensely, risking all you so profoundly love and hold dear. How could Free Solo be anything less than exhausting not only for Honnold, but equally for the photographers and director, who, as the film shows, are deeply conflicted by recording and enabling what could so easily be a wrenching tragedy. The film does attempt to explore the “why?” and pushes Honnold, not the most emotive of persons, for explanations that he is either unable or unwilling to share. He says simply that he is doing what he loves to do and is fortunate to be able to support what he acknowledges is his passion. Inherent in his choice, he admits, is the impact it has on those who care about him, especially his partner Sanni McCandless. It is her tears at the end of the film that are parenthetical to a reality she can’t bear to contemplate. It is an emotion that haunts this compelling, most amazing film. Free Solo. Documentary. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. View on VUDU, Prime Video. Alex Honnold in Free Solo.

articles.text: Berkeley Art Museum’s Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) is streaming a new documentary that profiles eight Bay Area artists. The film, Tell Them We Were Here, was created by Gallery 16 founder Griff Williams and filmmaker Keelan Williams, and made its worldwide debut in the virtual cinema of the BAMPFA. The film features local curators from BAMPFA, Oakland Museum and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA). It includes an appearance by filmmaker Eleanor Coppola, and Matt Gonzalez, chief attorney of the San Francisco Public Defender’s office, who is also an artist. The eight Bay Area artists highlighted in the documentary are Amy Franceschini, Sadie Barnette, Alicia McCarthy, Jim Goldberg, Tucker Nichols, Lynne Hershman Leeson, Nigel Poor, and Michael Swaine. The collection of art is a mix of photography, sculpting, podcasting, graffiti, and street art. The artists’ work spans decades and are considered to have made an emotional or cultural impact in the Bay Area. The film’s run time is 87 minutes, and has been available to stream since May 7 through BAMPFA’s virtual cinema. For streaming information, visit: https://bampfa.org/about/aboutbampfa.

articles.text: A scene from The Mitchells vs The Machines. Review by Chris Honoré Hollywood Writers have gotten a lot of mileage out of the dysfunctional family road trip, one that relies on a familiar trope: what can go wrong will go wrong, resulting, for the audience, in headshaking chuckles to outright laughter. At the center of The Mitchells vs The Machines is Katie Mitchell (Abbi Jacobson), a teen who loves movies, yearns to be a filmmaker, and dreams of moving to California, heartland of the fantasy industry. She lives with her mom, Linda (Maya Rudolph), maker of grotesquely charming cupcakes; a mutt named Monchi; her little brother Aaron (Mike Rianda), obsessed with dinosaurs; and her dad, Rick (Danny McBride), a hulking outdoors Mr. fix-it guy with whom she doesn’t quite feel at ease. But then he’s the kind of guy who gives you a non-slip screwdriver as a birthday gift, loves to build stuff, and worries that Katie’s dream of making movies will likely end in failure. He wonders where his little girl (who believed he could do anything) has gone, causing him to ask: who is this budding, newbie teenstranger called Katie? Inspired, Rick decides that what the family should do is not say goodbye to Katie at the airport as she heads off to college, but cancel her ticket and take a family road trip, giving them all a chance to reconnect. Katie is not so sure and is a little mortified at the thought of arriving at her new college with (gasp) her parents. Nevertheless, so begins a series of really “wide-eyed”, “good grief” misadventures from food poisoning to a visit to a seedy dinosaur theme park, and way more, all punctuated with minor family squabbles. articles.text: Mustang is a delight, stitched together with threads of melancholy. Directed and co-written by Deniz Erguven, a French-Turkish filmmaker and writer in her debut film, it’s in Turkish with an ensemble of five captivating actresses that enchant from the opening scenes. Each is remarkable. They portray sisters all in their early to mid teens – with the exception of Lale (Gunes Sensoy), who is perhaps 11 or 12. Each is brimming with youthful vitality and together they form a collective of willful sweetness that illustrates their bond as well as their rebelliousness. Each is coltish with rich, streaming hair, the intensity of their emotions palpable and wonderful. What is done to one is done to all, and though they argue and disagree, when faced with an impenetrable force like their grandmother (Nihal Koldas), they immediately form a united front. Orphaned when young, they are now being raised by their grandmother and uncle Erol (Aybeck Pekan). Though they vary in age, all, with the exception Lale, are on the cusp of young womanhood. Their youthful innocence is self-evident, their connection to one another unbreakable. The story takes place in a small town in northern Turkey on the Black Sea. It is the last day of school and summer stretches before them. Excited, filled with anticipation, they walk home with a group of boys along the shoreline of the ocean and end up splashing in the water, their uniforms drenched, some sitting on the shoulders of the boys as they try to push each other into the water. A neighbor sees them laughing and playing like young seals and reports their behavior to their grandmother who is scandalized and angry. She accuses them of pleasuring themselves while sitting on the shoulders of the boys – an idea completely foreign to the sisters. And so, the grandmother begins a campaign of cloistering the sisters as if they were nuns, having taken vows of chastity. With the uncle’s support, the grandmother begins to fashion their two-story house into a fortress, buttressing the walls, attempting to prevent every avenue of escape the girls might use to slip out into the night (or day). As well, she undertakes a program of preparing the girls for matrimony – cooking lessons, cleaning, sewing – an idea that shocks and even repels the sisters. Of course, both the uncle and grandmother are dealing with a collective life force, a blossoming sexuality that is culturally forbidden as a topic for discussion and behavior to be repressed at all cost. And so, what Lale regards as a “wife factory” is set in motion with the grandmother orchestrating arranged marriages for the older girls. In contrast, Lale can only think about escaping the fate that has descended on her muchloved sisters. She plots and plans her freedom, struggling with the cultural imperatives that confront every young Turkish woman. She begins a pitched, subversive battle to find an alternative for herself. She knows intuitively that she is facing a rigid (even violent), patriarchal future and rejects a life in which she has no choices. Mustang is a moving and engaging window into a culture far removed from the West. To the film’s credit, it avoids expository judgment; instead it allows circumstances and contrasts to carry and display a chasm of cultural differences in what proves to be a beautifully crafted and remarkable narrative. As an aside, Mustang was selected in 2015 as Best Foreign Language Film by the Academy of Motion Pictures. It is that good. Mustang. In Turkish with subtitles. Directed by Deniz Gamze Ergüven. Starring Gunes Senjoy, Tugba Sunguroglu, and Elit Iscan. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. A scene from Mustang.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its monthly Zoom book discussion on May 3, with 13 members in attendance to discuss Homegoing, a best seller. Participating were Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Margie Blodgett, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Maggie Blodgett, Karin Fetherston, Sally Arney, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Homegoing is Gha naian-American author Yaa Gyasi’s debut historical fiction novel published in 2016. The book’s title comes from an African-American belief that death allows an enslaved person’s spirit to travel back to Africa. Each chapter of the book follows a different descendant of an African Asante woman, starting with her two daughters. One marries the British governor in charge of the Cape Coast Castle, one of about 40 “slave castle” commercial forts that were built on the Gold Coast of West Africa by European slave traders. The other sister is held captive in the castle’s dungeons below and shipped off to America as a slave. The book follows seven generations of their children and covers 300 years. The 14 characters’ often tragic histories include Anglo-Asante wars in Ghana, and slavery and segregation in America. It was reported that Gyasi received a book advance of more than $1,000,000, enabling her to spend seven years researching the broad range of the book. It was selected in 2016 for the National heartaches, as well as the progress to the current day. Homegoing helped readers feel the emotions that these people experienced and better understand hard parts of our nation’s history as it relates to the treatment of African-Americans. The book, however, did not satisfy everyone. Some readers found the novel’s structure with alternating chapters of African and American characters difficult to follow, as well as to emotionally engage with the different characters. Some readers wanted to better understand them and know what happened in their lives after their chapters in the novel ended. This work of historical fiction has compressed nine generations and almost 300 years of African-American experiences in 320 pages – no mean feat. One reader said she liked the concept of the book more than the book itself. There was, however, agreement that Homegoing is an important book; it provides a set of human stories that give readers a more complete understanding of our racial past and the current state in which we live today. With their book conversation complete, the group discussed an offer from Piedmont writer and attorney Shanti Brian to have a discussion with her regarding her recently published book, Almost Innocent. Shanti is a practicing defense attorney and wife of a former NFL player. But you may not have kept up with some recent changes in the plan’s capabilities and in the educational environment in which the plan might be used. Let’s start with the learning environment. During the COVID- 19 pandemic, colleges and universities switched to online classes, or at least to a hybrid of in-person and online. And even before the pandemic, many schools offered remote classes, though obviously not to the same extent. But after COVID-19 subsides, it’s likely that the online component will remain an important part of higher education. What does this “new world” mean for you when you’re saving for college? Will a 529 plan still be relevant? In a word, yes. First of all, a 529 plan can offer tax advantages. Earnings in a 529 plan are federally tax-free, provided the money is used for qualified educational expenses. And if you invest in your own state’s 529 plan, your contributions may be tax deductible. (Withdrawals used for expenses other than qualified education expenses may be subject to federal and state taxes as well as a 10% penalty.) Because tax issues for 529 plans can be complex, you’ll want to consult with your tax advisor before investing. Online learning costs are eligible for a 529 plan’s tax benefits just as much as those incurred from in-person classes. Tuition, textbooks, supplies, computers and services – all of these should qualify, assuming the school meets certain criteria. Also, students enrolled half-time or more don’t have to live in a dorm for room and board expenses to be covered by a 529 plan – they can live in off-campus housing. However, these room-and-board costs typically must equal the cost of living on campus. Some schools identify a specific cost for “commuters” or “at-home students,” so you will need to contact the college directly to determine qualified room-and-board costs. Now, let’s take a quick look at what some changes in the rules governing 529 plans over the past few years might mean for you. Eligible expenses from your 529 plan include the following: • K-12 expenses – Parents can withdraw up to $10,000 per student, per year, from their 529 plan to pay for tuition expenses at elementary and secondary schools. So, if you intend to send your children to a private school, this use of a 529 plan might interest you. • Apprenticeships – 529 plans can be used to pay for fees, textbooks, equipment and other supplies connected to apprenticeship programs registered with the Department of Labor. These programs, typically offered at a community college, combine classroom instruction with on-the-job training. • Student loans – Families can withdraw funds from a 529 plan to repay the principal and interest for qualified education loans, including federal and most private student loans. There’s a lifetime limit of $10,000 for student loan repayments per each 529 plan beneficiary and another $10,000 for each of the beneficiary’s siblings. All of these newer uses of 529 plans may contain additional guidelines and exceptions, and state tax treatment varies, so you’ll want to consult with your tax advisor before taking money from your account. But it’s valuable for you to know the different ways you can put a 529 plan to work. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. T.J. FIRST MONDAY READING GROUP By Dick Carter The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group had its monthly Zoom book discussion on May 3, with 13 members in attendance to discuss Homegoing, a best seller. Participating were Mike Bandrowski, Melba Yee, Sarah Johnson, Laura Goldman, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Margie Blodgett, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Maggie Blodgett, Karin Fetherston, Sally Arney, Dick Carter, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Homegoing is Gha naian-American author Yaa Gyasi’s debut historical fiction novel published in 2016. The book’s title comes from an African-American belief that death allows an enslaved person’s spirit to travel back to Africa. Each chapter of the book follows a different descendant of an African Asante woman, starting with her two daughters. One marries the British governor in charge of the Cape Coast Castle, one of about 40 “slave castle” commercial forts that were built on the Gold Coast of West Africa by European slave traders. The other sister is held captive in the castle’s dungeons below and shipped off to America as a slave. The book follows seven generations of their children and covers 300 years. The 14 characters’ often tragic histories include Anglo-Asante wars in Ghana, and slavery and segregation in America. It was reported that Gyasi received a book advance of more than $1,000,000, enabling her to spend seven years researching the broad range of the book. It was selected in 2016 for the National First Monday Reading group tackles the best-selling Homegoing heartaches, as well as the progress to the current day. Homegoing helped readers feel the emotions that these people experienced and better understand hard parts of our nation’s history as it relates to the treatment of African-Americans. The book, however, did not satisfy everyone. Some readers found the novel’s structure with alternating chapters of African and American characters difficult to follow, as well as to emotionally engage with the different characters. Some readers wanted to better understand them and know what happened in their lives after their chapters in the novel ended. This work of historical fiction has compressed nine generations and almost 300 years of African-American experiences in 320 pages – no mean feat. One reader said she liked the concept of the book more than the book itself. There was, however, agreement that Homegoing is an important book; it provides a set of human stories that give readers a more complete understanding of our racial past and the current state in which we live today. With their book conversation complete, the group discussed an offer from Piedmont writer and attorney Shanti Brian to have a discussion with her regarding her recently published book, Almost Innocent. Shanti is a practicing defense attorney and wife of a former NFL player. In her book she writes about the criminal justice system as seen through her life experience, using the stories of nine of her previously convicted felon clients. articles.text: The Wednesday Evening Piedmont Meditation Group has moved online using Zoom web conferencing during the Covid-19 shelter-in-place order. The group meets every Wednesday evening from 7:30–8:15 p.m., and everyone age 12 and older is welcome. No experience meditating is necessary. This is a secular (non-religious) group, and there is no lecture, solicitation or obligation. Mark Herrick, a long-time Piedmont resident, is host of the weekly meditations. “With the high stress and anxiety of the shelter-in-place order, it’s easy to get cut-off and isolated from each other. It’s helpful to have a place to connect with people sharing a bit of quiet, peaceful time to rest and recharge,” Herrick said. For more information contact him at: herrickmark@icloud.com or (415) 706-2000.

articles.text: Ann Reynolds, a longtime Piedmont leader and educator, died peacefully on May 1st in her Piedmont home surrounded by her family after a valiant fight with pancreatic cancer. Born on January 8, 1935, she had a full, happy, and productive life and enjoyed every minute of it. With a smile that lit up a room, Ann was an adoring wife of 62 years, a loving mother and grandmother, a devoted daughter, and a joyful sister to her immediate family. As the glue to an extended family that included four generations of Reynolds and Seulbergers, she was the absolute center of the family universe, and a steward to so many more. She was seen as a champion in warmth, intelligence, humor, humanity, authenticity and certainly bravery right to the end. Ann lived a life of great purpose as she transformed her many passions into lasting contributions to her family, friends and community. Her infectious zest for life and the people in it became the fuel that changed the world in so many ways. Music, flowers, education and people were her love as she danced her way through life. As a curious and consummate learner, Ann was committed to not only her own education, but that of others. She studied at both Wellesley College and the University of California at Berkeley. She earned a masters of Science degree in Educational Psychology with a specialty in learning and a California school of counseling credential. Ann’s fervent commitment to education was the seed for several scholarships, and she delighted in interviewing amazing young people who not only loved learning but loved giving back. Ann’s dedication to Piedmont’s students, residents and causes reached far and wide. It began in 1959 as a math teacher at Piedmont High School, and later as a counselor and math teacher at Piedmont Middle School. When she moved to Piedmont with her husband Jon in 1974, Piedmont and education also as the co-founder of A Beautiful Night Housing in 2002, a non-profit committed to building a working farm for young adults with mental illness. Most recently, in July 2019 Ann co-founded LookUp.live with her daughter, Susan Reynolds, a non-profit venture to counter the impact of digital addiction and social isolation on youth mental health. She was integral to the successful launch of LookUp with an inaugural student-led campaign at Piedmont High and Millennium High, where students and adults alike took breaks from their phones for better tech-life balance. Ann had a deep love of flowers that began early with her father, J. Fred Seulberger, of Seulberger’s Flowers. She carried on his tradition through wildflower walks with her grandchildren and community members, sharing her Piedmont home on garden tours and as a board member of the Piedmont Garden Club and UC Botanical Garden. She was also an active member and avid supporter of the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and Piedmont Historical Society. Other things that brought joy to Ann’s life were golf, bridge, skiing, music and swing dancing. She brought passion and enthusiasm to all of her pursuits, and she shared them with family, friends and her community, including skiing with her grandchildren well into her 80’s. Ann is survived by her husband Jon Reynolds, her sister Jane Woodson, her three children, Susan Reynolds, Kassie Thomas (Bill), Jake Reynolds (Robin) and six grandchildren, Brittany Cappetta, Olivia Cappetta, Joseph Thomas, Sophie Reynolds, Annie Reynolds, and Zach Reynolds, and an extensive extended family. A small family service was held with plans for a Celebration of Ann’s life when Covid relents. Donations in Ann’s honor can be made to the Ann Reynolds Legacy Fund at www.LookUp.live, P.O. Box 1571, Concord, MA, 01742, or a charity of choice.
